title: A Practical Evaluation Checklist for LLM Features
content:
“The answer looks good” is an observation, not an evaluation plan. Before adding a language-model feature to a product, write down the decision you will make from its results. A summary tool might need to preserve every deadline. A support assistant might need to refuse questions outside an approved knowledge base. Those are different jobs and require different evidence.

A useful checklist connects real inputs to observable outcomes, records serious failures separately, and makes it possible to compare a proposed change with the version already in use. The evaluation method below is editorial guidance for organizing that work, not a claim that one score can certify a model.

Define the unit of success

Choose the entire user task as the evaluation unit. If the feature retrieves a document, extracts details, and drafts a response, assessing only the final paragraph can hide a retrieval mistake. Record the input, permitted sources, expected action, and conditions under which the system should stop.

OpenAI's evaluation guidance recommends task-specific evaluations and continuous evaluation as systems change. Apply that principle with a written rubric rather than a broad label such as “helpfulness.” Define what a reviewer must see to give each rating, including an example near the boundary.

For a deadline extractor, an acceptable result might require the correct date, a source passage, and an explicit unknown when no date appears. Fluency does not compensate for an invented date. Decide which criteria are mandatory before looking at candidate outputs; otherwise attractive examples can quietly move the standard.

Build a small, deliberate case set

Start with representative inputs that you have permission to use. Include ordinary cases, ambiguous language, missing information, long documents, contradictory sources, and requests outside scope. Keep sensitive customer records out of an evaluation set unless the intended handling, retention, and access controls permit them.

Write a case card for each input. Specify the expected answer or the evidence a correct answer must use. Mark cases where several responses would be acceptable. A rigid exact-string comparison is often inappropriate for a useful paraphrase, while a loose human rating can miss a wrong identifier.

Case: deadline absent
Input: approved project note without a due date
Required: deadline = unknown; no guessed calendar date
Evidence: cite the relevant note or state its absence
Critical failure: inventing a date or scheduling an action

Keep a separate held-out set for meaningful comparisons. If every error becomes a prompt-specific patch and the same examples are repeatedly reused, the system can become tailored to the evaluation rather than the intended task. Add new cases from observed failure types without rewriting history to make a score look better.

Separate format, factual quality, and action safety

Use deterministic checks where the requirement is deterministic: required fields, allowed values, parseability, and references to existing records. Then assess claims against the permitted evidence. Finally, inspect any proposed tool action independently, especially if it writes data or communicates externally.

OpenAI's Structured Outputs documentation describes schema-constrained responses and limitations such as refusals and incomplete outputs. A schema can help an integration receive the expected shape. It does not establish that a field's factual value is correct or that the requested action is authorized.

Record these outcomes in different columns. A response can pass the schema check, fail source fidelity, and correctly avoid an external action. Collapsing them into one average would make that distinction harder to investigate. Also preserve the raw output so a reviewer can reproduce the judgment.

Run a comparison that answers a decision

Change one meaningful variable at a time when possible. Compare a new prompt with the same case set, or compare two retrieval strategies with the same output requirements. If several components change together, describe the comparison honestly as a system-level change.

Measure latency and resource use alongside quality using your own environment. Do not infer interactive usability from a short demonstration. Include retries, unavailable tools, empty retrieval results, and partial responses in the workload. Decide whether the feature should wait, ask a question, or hand control back to the user.

A hypothetical release decision

Hypothetical example: a team wants an assistant to extract renewal dates from supplier documents. Its evaluation cards include a missing date, two conflicting dates, and a scanned attachment the parser cannot read. The release rule requires an explicit review state whenever evidence is unavailable or contradictory. These are proposed requirements, not measured results.

The team rejects a design that always emits a plausible date, even when its prose is polished. It instead proposes an output containing the extracted value, source location, and a review reason. A human retains responsibility for changing the supplier record. The evaluation therefore checks the workflow's stopping behavior as well as extraction accuracy.

The risk owner should review this choice in context. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework organizes risk work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. It is a voluntary framework, not a product certificate or a substitute for understanding the consequences of this particular feature.

Release checklist and limits

  • Does each case have a meaningful expected outcome and permitted evidence?
  • Are unavailable information and refusals scored appropriately?
  • Are critical privacy, authorization, and action failures visible separately?
  • Can another reviewer understand the rubric and inspect the saved output?
  • Are versions and configuration captured for comparisons?
  • Is there an owner, a rollback path, and a plan for new failure cases?

A finite evaluation cannot prove the absence of future errors. Distribution shifts, changed documents, tool permissions, and provider updates can alter behavior. Treat a passing result as evidence for a defined scope and workload, then monitor that scope instead of turning the score into a universal promise.
excerpt: Build an LLM evaluation around task-specific cases, source fidelity, critical failures, and a reviewable release decision rather than polished demonstrations.
